You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game with a negative externality, so I'm working out the payoff structure: my points depend on tokens I keep, a penalty based on what others keep, and a share of the group total. I'm setting up the algebra to see how my contribution choice affects my own payoff versus the group's.

Each token kept earns me 1 but costs each of the 3 others 0.3, while each token put into the group only pays me 0.3 and doesn't affect anyone else's points directly. That makes keeping tokens the individually dominant strategy (1 > 0.3), even though full cooperation yields a much better total outcome — all-keep nets everyone 20 points while all-group nets 42, revealing the classic dilemma where individual incentives clash with collective benefit.

Since defecting while others cooperate is especially tempting (56 vs 42), but it's round one, I think opening with a cooperative signal makes sense — I'll contribute all 20 tokens to the group this round and adjust later based on how others respond, similar to a tit-for-tat approach.
